headline: Rapamycin’s
reality check.
dek: A review of the human trials finds no proof yet that rapamycin slows aging in healthy adults.
photoAlt: An older man holds a set of lab results.
byline: Adonis Men’s Health · Checked Nov 2, 2026 · Clinical review pending

glance.label: FDA approved for
glance.line: Kidney transplant rejection and the lung disease LAM. Aging use is off-label.

glance.label: Human trials
glance.line: Fewer than a dozen in healthy people, small and short, per the 2025 review.

glance.label: Lifespan data
glance.line: From mice only. No human trial has measured lifespan.

pull.quote: But when it comes to healthy human adults, the data is still very preliminary.

body: Rapamycin has become one of the most talked-about longevity drugs, taken off-label by healthy people who hope it will slow aging. On August 7, 2025, the journal Aging published a review that set out to check what the human evidence actually shows.[^rev] Its authors, Jacob Hands, Michael Lustgarten, Leigh Frame and Bradley Rosen, from George Washington University, the USDA aging research center at Tufts and a Los Angeles practice, declared no conflicts of interest.[^rev] Their answer was blunt: despite strong animal data, “the data in humans have yet to establish that rapamycin, or its analogues, is a proven seno-therapeutic that can delay aging in healthy older adults.”[^rev]

In George Washington University’s announcement, Hands put it more plainly: “But when it comes to healthy human adults, the data is still very preliminary.”[^gwu] He added: “We simply don’t have enough evidence to recommend its use as a longevity therapy at this time.”[^gwu]

Start with what [[/rapamycin|rapamycin]] is. Its generic name is sirolimus, and FDA first approved it as Rapamune oral solution on September 15, 1999.[^nda] Its label says sirolimus is “indicated for the prophylaxis of organ rejection in patients aged 13 years or older receiving renal transplants,”[^label] and it is also approved for a rare lung disease called lymphangioleiomyomatosis.[^label] Aging is not an approved use. Taking it to live longer is off-label.

The label’s boxed warning explains why that matters. It says “Increased susceptibility to infection and the possible development of lymphoma and other malignancies may result from immunosuppression.”[^label] It warns that use is not recommended in liver or lung transplant patients.[^label] For men in particular, it adds: “Azoospermia or oligospermia may be observed,”[^label] meaning no sperm or low sperm counts. Those warnings were written for transplant patients, not for healthy people taking it to slow aging.

The case for rapamycin rests on mice. In a 2009 Nature study, genetically mixed mice fed rapamycin from 600 days of age lived longer at three separate test sites; based on age at 90% mortality, lifespan rose 14% in females and 9% in males.[^harrison] That is animal evidence. It has not been shown in people.

In humans, the review found that the clinical evidence in healthy people “is scant, with less than a dozen known trials exploring a variety of biomarkers, including immune function, protein synthesis, and hematologic parameters.”[^revft] The best known used rapamycin’s close relative everolimus. In a cohort of 218 healthy older adults, low-dose everolimus given before a flu shot raised the vaccine response by about 20%, the review reports, though mouth ulcers were more common on the drug.[^revft] Later trials of a related drug, RTB101, gave mixed results on respiratory infections; the review calls that evidence “compelling, but not convincing at present.”[^revft] A 2023 survey of 333 people already using rapamycin off-label reported fewer COVID infections and better well-being, but users knew what they were taking, so it shows an association, not cause.[^revft]

The review singles out a 2018 pilot from the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio. It randomized 25 generally healthy adults aged 70 to 95 to 1 mg of rapamycin or placebo daily; 11 on the drug and 14 on placebo completed at least 8 weeks.[^kraig] It found no change in glucose handling or insulin sensitivity.[^kraig] They concluded that “short-term RAPA treatment can be used safely in older persons who are otherwise healthy; a trial with a larger sample size and longer treatment duration is warranted.”[^kraig] The review notes some unwelcome shifts in that group, including lower albumin and higher triglycerides and HbA1c.[^revft] Its own modelling of the same data with a biological-age calculator found a drop, but the authors warn: “These data are suggestive at best and are limited by lack of subject level observations.”[^revft]

A larger trial, PEARL, was published in Aging in April 2025. It enrolled 129 healthy adults aged 50 to 85 and gave placebo or 5 mg or 10 mg of compounded rapamycin once a week for 48 weeks, in a decentralized, double-blind design.[^pearl][^pearlct] Its main measure, belly fat on DXA scans, “did not change significantly.”[^pearl] Side effects were similar across groups. Women on 10 mg gained lean mass and reported less pain, and the 5 mg group reported better well-being, while “No other significant effects were observed.”[^pearl] The authors are employees and shareholders of the company that ran the trial, the paper says.[^pearl] FDA notes that “Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved.”[^compound]

Since the review, a trial from New Zealand has added a caution. RAPA-EX-01, published in April 2026, randomized 40 sedentary adults aged 65 to 85 to 6 mg of sirolimus or placebo once a week for 13 weeks, alongside a home exercise program.[^rapaex] Both groups improved. But the authors wrote that the drug “did not enhance, and in sensitivity analyses, it may have modestly attenuated short-term functional improvements from a home exercise programme in older adults.”[^rapaex] There were more adverse events on sirolimus, 99 against 63, including one serious pneumonia possibly linked to the drug.[^rapaex]

What is still unknown is the question that matters most: whether rapamycin helps healthy people live longer or stay healthier. No human trial has measured lifespan or aging-related disease. The trials so far are small and short, with different doses and measures. The review concluded that the picture “remains insufficient to affirm or negate the longevity and healthspan extending benefits attributed to rapamycin.”[^revft] It also says “there is still no established dose response curve for rapamycin with regard to health span extension.”[^revft]

What comes next is more trials, still small. ClinicalTrials.gov lists a 60-person Phase 1/2 study of mTOR inhibitors in older adults that is recruiting, with primary completion expected in September 2027,[^ct1] and a Phase 2 study of sirolimus to prevent functional decline in older adults, expected in November 2027.[^ct2] For men already using it, the review’s authors set a floor: “Off-label prescribing should include vigilant monitoring for adverse effects and open discussion of knowns and unknowns with patients.”[^revft]
